title: The magic school of the future is one that helps students learn to work together and care for each other
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Bauschard argues that generative AI is collapsing the market value of the kind of analytical intelligence schools have long trained, so knowledge-worker wages and jobs are at risk. He surveys six themes in the AI-and-unemployment debate, from consensus that some jobs will vanish to optimism that new economic activity will replace them, and concludes that nobody credibly claims it will all simply work out. He then lists the challenges schools face: getting students and staff to use AI tools, training, resistance, AI literacy, and above all reorienting the system away from content-and-analysis. His central move is to redefine the purpose of school around human capacities machines cannot replace, namely collaboration, creativity, courage, and care for others. The piece is a school-focused call to reform in response to AI rather than a neutral forecast.
points: Cheap, abundant machine intelligence levels the advantage of the highest-IQ workers, as the BCG study showing the weakest employees gaining most is meant to illustrate.
The author sorts the unemployment debate into six themes and argues that the honest position is that a significant wave of job loss, at least in transition, is likely.
Getting tools into students' hands, training faculty, and building AI literacy are the easy challenges; reorienting what schools emphasize is the hard one.
Schools should shift from content and analysis toward communication, collaboration, critical thinking and creativity through project-based, interdisciplinary and experiential learning.
The closing claim is that the school worth building helps students care for each other, a role school staff are already prepared to play.
quotes: Now, machines can do many of the things we’ve traditionally defined as “intelligent,” and their ability to do so will grow rapidly. They already exceed human ability in these areas in many ways (no one knows as much as any AI across fields, and no one can discern patterns, analyze information, and make predictions as well as AIs can). If you need this type of intelligence, you can buy it, and you can buy it very, very cheaply.

The weakest employees gained the most, closing the gap with their more talented peers, who didn’t experience that much of a gain using it. AI works to level the unique value of intelligence in organizations.

The more difficult challenge is that we need to move the education system away from such a great emphasis on teaching content and analysis of content, as that type of “intelligence” isn’t going to have much economic value anymore.

We need to focus on helping students develop skills around communication, collaboration, critical thinking, and creativity (these will all be needed in humans even if the AI eventually develops them) and develop these skills (and relevant content knowledge) through project-based, interdisciplinary, and immersive/experiential learning experiences so they can fully develop and thrive as individuals who will co-exist with people (and robots) in a transformed world.

And we want to help children have courage, to have convictions, and to persevere. We humans will need these even if machines develop them. Machines can’t replace our courage, convictions, perseverance, and love.

Do schools have to focus on 1-5? No, they don’t. But if they don’t, they shouldn’t complain if kids don’t show up and are disengaged after they learn the basics of reading, writing, arithmetic, and the basics of how their society and economy work.
